CHAPTER 3.2 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.2 · LEARNING AREA 3 · APRIL · MAY

Surface area, volume and mass

Three equal pyramids fit exactly into a cube. From this follows a surprisingly simple formula for the volume of every pyramid. You calculate the surface area, volume and mass of prisms and pyramids, break difficult solids down into simple ones and get to know the frustum of a pyramid, which the ancient Egyptians could already calculate.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the surface area and volume of prisms
  • calculate the surface area and volume of pyramids and justify $V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$
  • calculate the mass of a solid from its volume and density
  • break composite solids down or complete them
  • know the frustum of a pyramid and calculate its volume
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

A triangle has a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 = 12$ cm²

What is the area of a square with side length 5 cm?

25 cm²

A cuboid is 5 cm, 4 cm and 3 cm long. Volume?

60 cm³

How many cubic centimetres are there in a cubic decimetre?

$1\,\text{dm}^3 = 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 10\,\text{cm}^3 = 1000\,\text{cm}^3$; that is one litre.

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Calculating prisms and pyramids

When you pour across, the pyramid fits into the prism exactly three times. That is no coincidence: a cube can be divided into three equal pyramids that all have their apex at the same corner. Each has a third of the volume of the cube.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA, VOLUME, MASS

Prism with the base $G$, the perimeter $u$ of the base and the height $h$: $\;M = u \cdot h$ (lateral surface) · $O = 2 \cdot G + M$ · $V = G \cdot h$

Pyramid with the base $G$ and the height $h$: $\;O = G + M$, the lateral surface $M$ is the sum of the lateral triangles · $V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$

For a regular pyramid with $n$ base edges $a$ and the height $h_s$ of the lateral triangles: $\;M = n \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot a \cdot h_s$

Mass: $\;m = \varrho \cdot V$ with the density $\varrho$ of the material.

Two heights: $h$ is the height of the pyramid, $h_s$ the height of a lateral triangle. $h_s$ is always greater than $h$.

Densities: spruce wood about $0.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, water $1\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, glass about $2.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$, steel about $7.85\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$.

INTERACTIVE · THREE PYRAMIDS, ONE CUBE
INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING SOLIDS

Choose a solid, its measurements and a material. The formulas and values are recalculated as you go.

EXAMPLE 1 · A TRIANGULAR PRISM

The base of a prism is a right-angled triangle with the sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. The prism is 10 cm high. Calculate $O$ and $V$.

$G = \tfrac12 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 6$ cm², $u = 12$ cm, $M = 12 \cdot 10 = 120$ cm².

$O = 2 \cdot 6 + 120 = 132$ cm² · $V = 6 \cdot 10 = 60$ cm³

EXAMPLE 2 · A STEEL PYRAMID

A square-based pyramid has $a = 6$ cm, $h = 4$ cm and $h_s = 5$ cm. Calculate $O$, $V$ and the mass if it is made of steel.

$G = 36$ cm², $M = 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 60$ cm², $O = 96$ cm². $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 48$ cm³.

$m = 7.85 \cdot 48 \approx 377$ g

EXERCISES

A triangular prism has as its base a triangle with $g = 5$ cm and $h_g = 4$ cm. It is 8 cm high. Calculate its volume.

$G = 10$ cm², $V = 10 \cdot 8 = 80$ cm³

A square-based pyramid has $a = 5$ cm and $h = 9$ cm. Calculate its volume.

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot 25 \cdot 9 = 75$ cm³

A square-based pyramid has $a = 10$ cm, $h = 12$ cm and $h_s = 13$ cm. Calculate the surface area and volume.

$O = 100 + 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 13 = 100 + 260 = 360$ cm². $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 100 \cdot 12 = 400$ cm³.

A wooden wedge is a triangular prism with $G = 12$ cm² and a length of 20 cm. How heavy is it if made of spruce ($\varrho = 0.5\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$)?

$V = 12 \cdot 20 = 240$ cm³, $m = 0.5 \cdot 240 = 120$ g

A pyramid has $V = 50$ cm³ and $G = 25$ cm². How high is it? How high would a prism with the same base and the same volume be?

Pyramid: $h = \tfrac{3V}{G} = \tfrac{150}{25} = 6$ cm. Prism: $h = \tfrac{V}{G} = 2$ cm, so a third as high.

TEST YOURSELF!

Prism with $G = 15$ cm² and $h = 4$ cm. Volume?

$15 \cdot 4 = 60$ cm³

Pyramid with $G = 12$ cm² and $h = 5$ cm. Volume?

$\tfrac13 \cdot 12 \cdot 5 = 20$ cm³

A solid has a volume of 30 cm³ and a density of $2\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$. How heavy is it?

$2 \cdot 30 = 60$ g

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Composite solids and the frustum of a pyramid

The block house consists of a cuboid and a roof in the shape of a triangular prism. Its volume is the sum of the two volumes. For the paint, however, only the faces on the outside count. The face on which the roof rests is not painted.

KEY POINT · REDUCING TO KNOWN SOLIDS, AND THE FRUSTUM

Breaking down: divide the solid into known solids and add their volumes. Completing: complete it to a known solid and subtract what is too much.

For the surface area only the faces on the outside count.

If you cut through a pyramid parallel to the base, you get a frustum at the bottom. The base and the top face are parallel and have the same shape; the lateral faces are trapeziums. Its volume: $\;V = V_{\text{whole pyramid}} - V_{\text{top cut off}}$.

Sketch first: Draw the solid and mark the parts in colour before you calculate.

Trapezium: $A = \tfrac{a + c}{2} \cdot h$. This is how you calculate the lateral faces of the frustum.

INTERACTIVE · THE FRUSTUM OF A PYRAMID

Change the base edge, the top edge and the height. The volume comes out as large pyramid minus small top.

EXAMPLE 3 · A HOUSE

A house is a cuboid (8 m wide, 6 m deep, 5 m high) with a gable roof. The gable triangles have a 6 m base and a height of 3 m. Calculate the volume.

Cuboid: $8 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 240$ m³. Roof: prism with $G = \tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 3 = 9$ m² and a length of 8 m: $72$ m³.

$V = 240 + 72 = 312$ m³

EXAMPLE 4 · A FRUSTUM OF A PYRAMID

A square frustum has an edge length of 4 cm at the bottom and 2 cm at the top and is 6 cm high. The whole pyramid would be 12 cm high. Calculate the volume.

Whole pyramid: $\tfrac13 \cdot 16 \cdot 12 = 64$ cm³. Top: $\tfrac13 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 8$ cm³.

$V = 64 - 8 = 56$ cm³

EXERCISES

On a cube with edge length 6 cm sits a square-based pyramid with the same base and a height of 4 cm. Calculate the volume of the whole solid.

$216 + \tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 4 = 216 + 48 = 264$ cm³

The pyramid from exercise 6 has lateral triangles with $h_s = 5$ cm. Calculate the surface area of the whole solid. Which face does not count?

The top face of the cube and the base of the pyramid lie inside. $O = 5 \cdot 36 + 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 = 180 + 60 = 240$ cm².

A square hole with side length 2 cm goes from top to bottom through a cuboid (10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm). Calculate the volume.

Complete and subtract: $480 - 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6 = 456$ cm³.

A square frustum has an edge length of 6 cm at the bottom and 3 cm at the top and is 4 cm high. The whole pyramid would be 8 cm high. Calculate its volume.

Whole pyramid $\tfrac13 \cdot 36 \cdot 8 = 96$ cm³, top $\tfrac13 \cdot 9 \cdot 4 = 12$ cm³. $V = 84$ cm³.

The trapeziums of this frustum are about 4.3 cm high. Calculate its surface area.

Lateral surface: $4 \cdot \tfrac{6 + 3}{2} \cdot 4.3 = 77.4$ cm². $O = 36 + 9 + 77.4 \approx 122$ cm².

TEST YOURSELF!

A cube with a 4 cm edge carries a pyramid with $G = 16$ cm² and $h = 3$ cm. Total volume?

$64 + 16 = 80$ cm³

The whole pyramid has a volume of 100 cm³, the top cut off 12 cm³. Volume of the frustum?

88 cm³

A trapezium has the parallel sides 6 cm and 2 cm and a height of 5 cm. Area?

$\tfrac{6 + 2}{2} \cdot 5 = 20$ cm²

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Convert: a) 2.5 dm³ into cm³   b) 3500 cm³ into litres   c) 1 m³ into litres

a) 2500 cm³   b) 3.5 ℓ   c) 1000 ℓ

A tent is a triangular prism: the gable triangle has a 1.6 m base and a height of 1.2 m; the tent is 2 m long. The sloping sides are each 1.44 m wide. Calculate the volume and the fabric needed without the floor.

$V = \tfrac12 \cdot 1.6 \cdot 1.2 \cdot 2 = 1.92$ m³. Fabric: two roof surfaces $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1.44 = 5.76$ m² and two gables $2 \cdot 0.96 = 1.92$ m², together $7.68$ m².

Connecting with chapter 2.3: A square-based pyramid has $V = 72$ cm³ and $a = 6$ cm. Rearrange $V = \tfrac13 G h$ for $h$ and calculate the height.

$h = \tfrac{3V}{G} = \tfrac{216}{36} = 6$ cm

Connecting with chapter 2.4: Every edge of a cube becomes 10% longer. By what percentage does its volume grow? And its surface area?

Volume: $1.1^3 = 1.331$, so by 33.1%. Surface area: $1.1^2 = 1.21$, so by 21%.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A frustum of a pyramid on papyrus

In the Pushkin Museum in Moscow there is an ancient Egyptian papyrus with 25 mathematical problems, the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus. It was written around 1850 BC; the dates given vary a little.

Problem 14 asks for the volume of a frustum of a pyramid: 6 high, with side 4 at the bottom and side 2 at the top. The scribe calculates by a recipe: 4 times 4 gives 16, 4 times 2 gives 8, 2 times 2 gives 4. Together 28. A third of 6 is 2. And 28 times 2 is 56.

That is exactly the result of Example 4, which you found as the large pyramid minus the small top. To this day nobody knows for certain where the Egyptians got their recipe from.

Source: Moscow Mathematical Papyrus, problem 14, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow.
